data.text/markdown:
Forward kinematics of robot arms

Forward (or direct) kinematics answers: given the joint values ||(q = (q_1, \dots, q_n)||), where is the tool? With one Denavit-Hartenberg transformation ||(A_i(q_i)||) per link (see the DH parameters notebook), the pose of the tool in the base frame is their composition: ||[T_0^n(q) = A_1(q_1) \oplus A_2(q_2) \oplus \dots \oplus A_n(q_n)||]This notebook computes it with the MRPT Python wheel (pip install mrpt3), where every ||(A_i||) is an mrpt.poses.CPose3D and ||(\oplus||) is the + operator. It shows:
  1. The pose of the tool for any joint values, for six classic robots.
  2. The workspace: all the points the tool can reach.
  3. Velocity kinematics: the Jacobian, the velocity ellipsoid, and the singular configurations where the robot loses mobility.
The inverse kinematics notebook solves the opposite problem.

1. From joint values to the tool pose

Choose a robot and move the joint sliders. The figure shows the DH skeleton of the arm (gray), its revolute (circles) and prismatic (diamonds) joints, the frame of every link and, larger, the tool frame ||(T_0^n||). Drag the figure to rotate it.

data.text/markdown:
2. The workspace

The workspace is the set of all positions the tool can reach. A simple way to see it is to draw many random joint configurations, within the joint limits, and plot where the tool ends up. Its shape gives the robot family its name: an annulus for the planar arm, a cylinder shell for the cylindrical robot, a thick sphere for the anthropomorphic arm... The points are colored by the manipulability of their configuration (section 3): it drops near the borders of the workspace, where the arm is stretched or folded.

data.text/markdown:
3. Velocity kinematics and singularities

How fast does the tool move when the joints move? Differentiating the forward kinematics gives a linear relation, through the geometric Jacobian ||(J(q)||), a ||(6 \times n||) matrix: ||[\begin{bmatrix} v \\ \omega \end{bmatrix} = J(q)\, \dot q, \qquad J_i = \begin{cases} \begin{bmatrix} z_{i-1} \times (o_n - o_{i-1}) \\ z_{i-1} \end{bmatrix} & \text{revolute joint} \\[2mm] \begin{bmatrix} z_{i-1} \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} & \text{prismatic joint} \end{cases}||]where ||(v||) and ||(\omega||) are the linear and angular velocities of the tool, and ||(z_{i-1}||), ||(o_{i-1}||) the axis and origin of frame ||(i-1||), all read from the CPose3D frames of section 1. Below, ||(J||) is compared with numerical derivatives of the forward kinematics. The singular values of ||(J||) tell how easily the tool moves in each direction. At a singular configuration some of them vanish: the rank of ||(J||) drops and the tool cannot move in some direction, whatever the joint speeds. The velocity ellipsoid, the set of tool velocities ||(v||) reachable with ||(\|\dot q\| \le 1||), then collapses into a flat shape. Try these singularities with the sliders of section 1:
  • Planar 3R arm: ||(\theta_2 = 0°||), the first two links aligned.
  • Anthropomorphic arm: ||(\theta_5 = 0°||) (wrist: axes 4 and 6 aligned) or ||(\theta_3 = 90°||) (elbow: arm fully stretched).
  • UR5: ||(\theta_5 = 0°||) (wrist) or ||(\theta_3 = 0°||) (elbow).
